sections.title: What is a Fenwick Tree / BIT?
sections.content:
A Fenwick Tree (also called a Binary Indexed Tree or BIT) is a compact data structure that supports two operations on an array: **prefix sum query** (sum of elements from index 1 to i) in O(log n) and **point update** (add a delta to element i) in O(log n). It was introduced by Peter Fenwick in 1994 as a simpler and more cache-friendly alternative to segment trees for the specific case of prefix sums.

It is not a tree in the traditional sense - it is a flat array with a clever indexing scheme. The magic comes from the expression `i & (-i)`, which in two's complement isolates the **lowest set bit** of `i`. This single operation determines how many elements each index is responsible for, and drives both the query and update traversals.

The result is a structure that requires less code than a segment tree, uses roughly half the memory, and is faster in practice due to better cache behavior. The trade-off: it is less general. A BIT natively supports prefix queries (not arbitrary range aggregation) and works cleanly for sum and XOR. Extending it to range min/max requires extra tricks, whereas a segment tree handles those naturally.

BITs show up in competitive programming whenever you need **inversion count**, **count of smaller elements dynamically**, or **prefix sums with updates**.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use a Fenwick Tree when you need prefix sum queries with point updates, and the operation is sum or XOR. It is the go-to for inversion counting (coordinate compress + BIT) and for order statistics on a dynamic stream of insertions. Prefer it over a segment tree when the problem fits, because the implementation is shorter and faster. If you need range min/max with updates, or range updates with range queries, use a segment tree instead.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## The BIT Array and Responsibility

Position `i` in the BIT stores the sum of a specific range ending at `i`. The range length is determined by `i & (-i)` - the value of the lowest set bit of `i`. For example:
- `i = 6` → binary `110` → `6 & -6 = 2` → stores sum of 2 elements: `arr[5..6]`
- `i = 8` → binary `1000` → `8 & -8 = 8` → stores sum of 8 elements: `arr[1..8]`

This overlapping responsibility means any prefix sum `[1..i]` can be reconstructed by summing at most `log(n)` BIT positions.

## Query - Prefix Sum [1..i]

Start at index `i`. Add `bit[i]` to the running sum. Move to `i - (i & -i)` - this strips the lowest set bit, jumping to the next position responsible for a range ending before the current range. Repeat until `i` reaches 0. At most `log(n)` iterations.

## Update - Add Delta to Position i

Start at index `i`. Add `delta` to `bit[i]`. Move to `i + (i & -i)` - this adds the lowest set bit, propagating the change to all BIT positions whose responsibility range includes `i`. Repeat until `i > n`. At most `log(n)` iterations. Note the direction is **opposite** to query: query goes left (strip bit), update goes right (add bit).

## Range Sum and Difference BIT

To query the sum of an arbitrary range `[l, r]`: compute `query(r) - query(l - 1)`. This is not a single traversal but two prefix queries.

For **range update + point query** (the inverse problem - add `v` to all elements in `[l, r]`, then read a single element), use a **difference BIT**: apply `update(l, v)` and `update(r + 1, -v)`. Then `query(i)` gives the effective value at position `i`.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Standard 1-indexed Fenwick Tree supporting O(log n) point updates and prefix sum queries. The `rangeSum` method combines two prefix queries. Build from an existing array using the `buildBIT` helper in O(n log n).

items.name: 2D Fenwick Tree
items.description: Extends BIT to a 2D grid for rectangle sum queries with point updates. Both update and query run in O(log(rows) * log(cols)). The implementation nests two BIT loops: outer loop over rows, inner loop over columns.

items.name: Range Update + Range Query BIT
items.description: Uses two BITs (B1 and B2) to support both range updates and range queries in O(log n) each. The math: prefix sum with range updates can be expressed as a function of two BIT prefix sums. More complex than standard BIT but avoids needing a segment tree.

items.name: BIT for Order Statistics (Coordinate Compressed)
items.description: Coordinate-compress the values into [1..n], then use a BIT where position `v` represents 'how many times value v has been inserted so far.' A prefix sum query gives the count of inserted elements <= v. This solves inversion count and 'count of smaller numbers after self.'
items.example_problem: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

items.name: Difference BIT (Range Update + Point Query)
items.description: To add `v` to all elements in [l, r]: call `update(l, v)` and `update(r+1, -v)` on a difference BIT. Then `prefixSum(i)` gives the effective value at position `i`. This is the inverse of the standard BIT use case.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n log n) build, O(log n) update, O(log n) prefix query
sections.explanation: Each update or query traversal moves along the binary representation of the index, either stripping or adding the lowest set bit. An n-bit index can undergo at most n such operations, giving O(log n) per operation. Building from an array calls update n times: O(n log n). There is an O(n) build possible by direct construction, but the update-based build is standard. Space is exactly n+1 integers for the BIT array.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: BIT is 1-indexed - accessing `bit[0]` is either unused or causes bugs. When your array is 0-indexed, always shift by +1 when calling `update` and `prefixSum`. Forgetting this shift gives wrong counts silently.
Confusing query direction with update direction - query strips the lowest set bit (`i -= i & -i`, moving left), update adds it (`i += i & -i`, moving right). Mixing them produces garbage results.
BIT natively gives only prefix sums - range [l, r] requires `query(r) - query(l-1)`. Calling `query(r - l)` or similar is wrong and a common mistake under pressure.

Coordinate compression required for values outside [1..n] - if you're counting 'how many elements smaller than x' where x can be any integer, compress values to [1..n] first. Skipping this leads to out-of-bounds BIT access or incorrectly sized arrays.

Forgetting `i & (-i)` in JS works on 32-bit signed integers - for `n` larger than 2^30, the lowest-set-bit calculation can overflow into negative numbers. For typical interview constraints (n <= 10^5) this is not an issue, but be aware.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.next_topic: Advanced Graph - Bridges, Articulation Points, SCC
sections.why: After mastering tree-based data structures for range queries, the next step in Level 7 is advanced graph algorithms. These require deep DFS understanding - tracking discovery times and low values - which builds on the recursive thinking used in segment trees and BIT.
